opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because the interface is really where the leverage is. The models are getting good enough that the bottleneck isn't "can the agent do the task," it's "can the human stay meaningfully in the loop without becoming the bottleneck themselves."

So the way I'd frame it: the researcher should feel like a PI running a lab, not like someone babysitting a chatbot. That means a few things.

First, the unit of interaction should be the research question or hypothesis, not the individual prompt. You want to say, "Here's what I'm trying to figure out, here's what I already believe, here's what would change my mind," and then let agents fan out and pursue different threads. The UI should make that tree of work visible: what's being explored, what's been ruled out, and why.

Second, you need really good surfacing of the moments that actually need human judgment. Agents will generate enormous amounts of intermediate output, and nobody's going to read all of it. The system's job is to compress that and say, "Here are the three decisions that matter, here's the evidence on each side, here's where the agents disagree or where confidence is low." Disagreement between agents is actually one of the most useful signals you can show a researcher.

Third, provenance and auditability. If an agent makes a claim, I want to click through and see exactly what it ran, what data it looked at, what assumptions it made. Trust has to be earned incrementally, and you can't earn it if the reasoning is a black box. Over time, as a researcher sees an agent being reliable on certain kinds of tasks, they should be able to grant it more autonomy there, kind of like how you'd give a grad student more rope as they prove themselves.

And finally, steering should be cheap. If I look at something and think, "No, that's the wrong direction," redirecting shouldn't mean starting over. I should be able to annotate, prune a branch, inject a constraint, and have that propagate.

The overall goal is to amplify the researcher's taste. The agents bring breadth and speed; the human brings judgment about what's interesting and what's true. The UX should be designed around protecting and leveraging that judgment, rather than replacing it.

r001.rationale: It says the researcher should act like a PI running a lab and direct agents as they fan out across research threads.

r002.rationale: It supports auditing by inspecting what an agent ran, its data, and assumptions, but does not clearly say researchers can inspect the underlying code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest starting point is that we don't fully know yet, and anyone who tells you they've nailed the interface for this is probably overselling. But I can tell you how we think about it.

The core thing we're trying to avoid is the "chat box with a very smart intern" model, where you type a question, wait, get a wall of text back, and then have to re-explain everything the next time. That works fine for one-off tasks. It falls apart completely when you're running an actual research program, where the work happens over weeks, there are dozens of threads going at once, and the important state is not in any single conversation but in the accumulated understanding of what's been tried and why.

So the first principle is that the unit of organization is the research question, not the conversation. When a scientist comes into Silico, they should see their hypotheses, the experiments that have been run against them, what the results were, and what's currently in flight. The agents are doing the work underneath that structure, but the human is looking at the science, not at the agents.

The second principle is what I'd call graduated autonomy. Early on, with a new user or a new line of inquiry, the system should be checking in a lot. "Here's the experimental design I'm proposing, here's why, here are the alternatives I rejected." The researcher approves, modifies, or redirects. As trust builds and the system learns how this particular scientist thinks about tradeoffs, those checkpoints get sparser. You move from approving every step to approving the plan to just reviewing results. But the dial should always be visible and the human should be the one turning it.

Third, and this is the one I think people underweight, is that the interface has to make disagreement easy. A researcher needs to be able to look at what an agent concluded and say "no, I think you're wrong about this, here's why," and have that actually propagate. Not just get a polite "you're right, I apologize" and then the same mistake three steps later. The system should treat the human's scientific judgment as a first-class input that updates its model of the problem, and it should be able to push back too, with evidence, when it thinks the researcher is wrong. The best collaborations I've had with human colleagues involved a lot of productive arguing, and I don't see why this should be different.

And then the last piece is legibility of the long tail. The agents are going to do a lot of stuff the researcher will never look at closely, and that's fine, that's the point. But when something surprising shows up, the scientist has to be able to pull the thread all the way back. What data was this based on, what assumptions went into the analysis, what did the agent consider and discard. If you can't audit it, you can't trust it, and if you can't trust it you shouldn't be publishing off it.

So the short version is: organize around the science, let the human set the autonomy level, make disagreement a real channel in both directions, and make everything traceable when it matters. We're probably getting a bunch of the details wrong right now and we'll find out by watching real scientists use it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a researcher directing agent work and setting autonomy, but does not clearly propose a principal-investigator role orchestrating a large team of agents.

r002.rationale: It says researchers should trace results to data, assumptions, and discarded alternatives, but does not mention inspecting the underlying code.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make the researcher’s intent the organizing principle of the experience. You should be able to say, “Here’s the question I’m trying to answer, here are my constraints, and here’s what would count as convincing evidence,” and then work with the agents to turn that into a plan.

And you need meaningful opportunities to steer. You don’t want to approve every little action, but you do want an agent to surface an assumption that could change the direction of the research. The interface should make it easy to understand what’s happening, inspect the evidence behind a conclusion, and say, “Actually, let’s pursue this other explanation.”

So I’d think of it as a workspace for an ongoing scientific conversation. The agents can take on more of the execution, while the researcher stays engaged with the questions, the judgment calls, and what the results actually mean.

r001.rationale: The response describes a researcher guiding agents and steering their work, but does not communicate orchestrating a large team of AI research agents.

r002.rationale: It mentions inspecting evidence behind conclusions, but does not say researchers can inspect the underlying code to verify results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to keep the researcher in control of the scientific direction without making them micromanage every action. You should be able to say, “Here’s the question I’m trying to answer, here are my constraints,” and have the agents propose a plan that you can inspect and adjust.

Then, as they work, the interface should make it easy to understand what they’ve done, what evidence they’re using, and where they’re uncertain. You want to be able to interrupt and say, “That assumption doesn’t make sense,” or, “This result is interesting—let’s follow that.”

So I think it’s less about having a chat window where you ask for something and wait for an answer, and more about creating a shared workspace where the research stays visible and steerable. The agents can handle a lot of the execution, but the human should always be able to exercise scientific judgment.

r001.rationale: The response describes a researcher setting direction and steering agents, but does not convey orchestrating a large team of AI research agents in a principal-investigator-like role.

r002.rationale: It mentions inspecting agents’ plans, evidence, and work, but does not say researchers can inspect the underlying code to verify reported results.
